stories.title: Salesforce Completes $3.6B Acquisition of Fin (Formerly Intercom Fin), Adding 30K AI Customers to Agentforce
stories.body: Salesforce completed its acquisition of Fin, formerly Intercom, on September 10, 2026, paying approximately $3.6 billion and bringing Fin's customer agent platform and more than 30,000 business customers into its Agentforce ecosystem. Fin's AI agent — powered by a proprietary model called Apex, purpose-built for support — claims to resolve 76% of incoming support requests without a human agent. Salesforce has folded Fin's technology into Agentforce, framing the combination as giving enterprises faster, more flexible ways to deploy trusted AI agents across customer service operations.
stories.why: Fin is now a Salesforce product, meaning every retail enterprise running Salesforce CRM will have a bundled agent option pitched to them — this reshapes competitive dynamics for any standalone agent vendor and changes the 'build vs. buy vs. bundle' conversation on a call. Salesforce's framing — 'measurable outcomes at scale' — is exactly the language Graas must match with grounded, context-layer proof rather than marketing claims.

stories.title: McKinsey 'State of AI 2026': 32% of Enterprises Skipped a Software Purchase to Build With Agentic Coding Tools; Only 6% Qualify as AI High Performers
stories.body: McKinsey's State of AI 2026 report — fielded May–June 2026 across 1,719 respondents in 97 countries — found that 32% of organizations decided against buying at least one software product or feature because they could build it in-house using agentic coding tools, with the figure rising to nearly 50% among AI high performers. Separately, only 6% of respondents qualify as AI high performers (attributing ≥5% of EBIT to AI), a figure flat since 2025, and only 37% can attribute any earnings impact at all. Among enterprises with over $1 billion in revenue, those scaling AI agents rose from 27% to 40% in a single year.
stories.why: The build-vs-buy finding is the most dangerous objection a Graas seller will face in 2026: prospects will cite McKinsey to justify building in-house rather than buying a retail AI solution. The parallel finding — that 94% of enterprises are spending on AI without moving earnings — is the strongest counter-argument: context-layer and agent infrastructure built by specialists, not internal teams, is what separates the 6% who actually win.

stories.title: McKinsey Agentic Commerce Consumer Survey (Oct 28, 2026): Retailer AI Platforms Outperform Standalone AI at Point of Purchase Because of Live Infrastructure
stories.body: Published October 28, 2026, McKinsey's Agentic Commerce Consumer Survey found that for AI users, AI search is three times more influential than traditional search, and that sectors with traditionally low e-commerce penetration — such as grocery and beauty — are catching up quickly through agentic commerce. A key structural finding: retailer AI assistants outperform standalone AI platforms at the point of purchase because retail AI platforms already have infrastructure in place for live inventory, payments, and delivery. McKinsey estimates that widespread adoption of agentic commerce could increase US e-commerce sales by 11.5% above baseline forecasts by 2030.
stories.why: McKinsey's infrastructure-wins argument is a direct brief for Graas: retailers that lack a connected context layer — live inventory, pricing logic, product taxonomy — will lose agent-mediated purchases to those that have it. A seller can quote this finding directly to a CMO or CTO to justify the data foundation investment before deploying any agent.

stories.title: Siemens RapidMiner Publishes Architecture Brief: Knowledge Graph as the Context Layer Every Agentic AI Initiative Requires
stories.body: A Siemens RapidMiner technical brief (published ~9 days ago) argues that an enterprise knowledge graph is the context layer for every agentic AI initiative an organization will ever run, functioning as a semantic overlay that sits above existing platforms — Databricks, Snowflake, Microsoft Fabric, AWS, and SAP — connecting and contextualizing operational data in place rather than moving it. The brief distinguishes a 'context graph' (for structured, relationship-rich operational data agents must reason across) from a vector store or graph database, and positions its Graph Studio product as that production-grade layer. The core claim: enterprise AI does not have a model problem — it has a context problem, and agents that lack this layer reason within domains rather than across them.
stories.why: This is the architectural argument Graas makes on every call: agents fail not because models are weak but because they lack a trusted, queryable map of the business. Siemens (a credible industrial and enterprise brand) publishing this framing validates the context-layer narrative and gives sellers a vendor-neutral third-party reference for why the data foundation must come before agent deployment.

stories.title: Sierra Raises $950M at $15.8B; Decagon at $4.5B — Outcome-Based Pricing and Competing Architectures Now Define the Enterprise Agent Market
stories.body: Sierra raised $950 million led by Tiger Global and GV in May 2026 at a $15.8 billion valuation — the largest in the enterprise agent category — after reporting $150 million in ARR in February; its per-resolution pricing is estimated at ~$1.50 by third parties, since Sierra does not publish its rate. Decagon tripled its valuation to $4.5 billion in a $250 million Series D in January 2026, and in March 2026 added persistent memory across conversations and outbound voice calls; its Duet Autopilot feature tunes agents with less human setup. The two companies now define opposite build philosophies: Sierra deploys its own team alongside the customer using Ghostwriter and Agent Studio; Decagon relies on versioned Agent Operating Procedures configured by the buyer's team.
stories.why: Sierra and Decagon are the most likely names a retail enterprise prospect will have already seen before a Graas call — knowing their pricing models, architectural choices, and gaps (neither publishes a context-layer or knowledge-graph grounding story) lets a seller redirect the conversation toward what agents need underneath to reliably resolve complex retail queries like substitutions, inventory eligibility, and loyalty logic.
